parole.significato: keg, cask (large barrel for the storage of liquid)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian бандура (bandura), from Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra).
Borrowed from Ukrainian букша (bukša), from German Büchse, from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā, from Late Latin buxis. Doublet of pușcă and boxă. This influenced or merged with several variants of bucea.
Borrowed from Ukrainian буга́й (buháj), from a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *buka.

Borrowed from Ukrainian бутелка (butelka), from Polish butelka, from butla, from German Buttel, from French bouteille, from Late Latin butticula, from buttis (“cask, barrel”). Doublet of butelie and bute.
Borrowed from Ukrainian катеринка (katerynka), from French Catherine, as one of the first songs to be played on the barrel organ was Charmante Catherine. Compare Russian шарманка (šarmanka).

parole.significato: long peasant's mantle worn by women

Borrowed from Ukrainian чорнушка (čornuška) or Russian чернушка (černuška).
Borrowed from Ukrainian кисляк (kysljak), from Proto-Slavic *kyslъ (“sour”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian чоботи (čoboty), plural of чобіт (čobit).
Borrowed from Ukrainian ко́бза (kóbza), from Proto-Turkic *kopuŕ.
Borrowed from Ukrainian конар (konar), from Proto-Slavic *konarъ.
Unknown. Possibly from Ukrainian косар (kosar), or an internal derivation, coasă + -ar, in both cases ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kosa (“scythe”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian ко́цур (kócur) of the same meaning.

Borrowed from Ukrainian голка (holka), from Proto-Slavic *gъlkъ, *gъlka.
Borrowed from Ukrainian горн (horn), from Proto-Slavic *gъrnъ.
Borrowed from Ukrainian грани́ця (hranýcja). Doublet of graniță.
Borrowed from Ukrainian гриб (hryb), from Proto-Slavic *gribъ (“mushroom”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian груба (hruba), from German Grube.
Borrowed from Ukrainian голуб (holub), from Proto-Slavic *golǫbь.

parole.significato: salt obtained by boiling salty springs

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian хитрий (xytryj), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ. Compare Bulgarian хитър (hităr), Russian хитрый (xitryj), Czech chytrý, Old Church Slavonic хꙑтръ (xytrŭ).
Borrowed from Ukrainian ярмарок (jarmarok), from Polish jarmark, from German Jahrmarkt (“fair”).
Unknown. Possibly from Ukrainian живе́ць (žyvécʹ, “fry, small fish”), from Baltic (compare Lithuanian žuvi̇̀s, Latvian zivs, both ‘fish’), with suffix altered to diminutive -ete.
Borrowed from Ukrainian лях (ljax), from Old Ruthenian лѧхъ (ljax), from Old East Slavic лѧхъ (lęxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lęxъ, from Proto-Slavic *lęděninъ (“dweller of wasteland”).
liur (“weak, poor wine”), of Ukrainian origin + -că.

Borrowed from Ukrainian урядник (urjadnyk) or Russian урядник (urjadnik). First attested in 1621

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian торопити (toropyty). Compare Russian торопеть (toropetʹ, “to be bewildered, confused”).

Borrowed from Ukrainian валом (valom), from вал (val).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian цидула (cydula), from Polish cedula, from Medieval Latin cedula, from Latin schedula, from Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”). Compare Russian цидула (cidula), Hungarian cédula, German Zettel.
